query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Integrating an in‐situ powder bed preheating step during laser powder bed fusion will reduce thermal gradients and residual stresses during fabrication of high‐entropy alloy components, thereby improving dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while simultaneously reducing fabrication‐induced defects.
generation.material_initial_state: High‐entropy alloy components produced by standard LPBF processing without powder bed preheating, which typically exhibit significant porosity, thermal stress‐induced distortions, and microscale defects.
generation.intervention: Modify the LPBF process by preheating the powder bed to a moderate, controlled temperature (e.g., 400–600 °C) in an inert (argon) atmosphere before and during laser exposure.
generation.conditions: Processing is carried out via LPBF on refractory or eutectic high‐entropy alloys under standard laser power and scanning speed conditions. The preheating is applied consistently throughout the build in a controlled inert environment to minimize oxidation risks, and the process is implemented on powders with low oxygen content.
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients induced by preheating are expected to lower residual stresses and stabilize the microstructural evolution (potentially promoting beneficial short‐range order), which in turn limits rapid solidification defects such as porosity and microcracking.
generation.mechanism: Preheating diminishes the thermal shock and abrupt cooling inherent in LPBF, leading to a slower, more uniform solidification. This moderates contraction stresses, decreases defect nucleation (e.g., porosity and cracking), and may subtly influence short‐range ordering that stabilizes dislocation motion, collectively enhancing mechanical integrity and dimensional accuracy.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to conventional LPBF parts, components fabricated with powder bed preheating should exhibit lower porosity and residual stresses, reduced warpage/distortion (improved dimensional precision), and a measurable improvement in mechanical properties (e.g., yield or compressive strength potentially 10–20% higher), though the exact magnitude requires empirical validation.
generation.baseline: LPBF‐fabricated high‐entropy alloy components produced without any powder bed preheating, which serve as the standard process benchmark with known issues of dimensional distortions and fabrication‐induced defects.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of this intervention is expected to be limited to alloy systems that tolerate elevated temperatures without oxidation or unwanted phase transformations. Excessive preheating may lead to powder coalescence or deleterious microstructural changes; thus, the optimal preheating window must be adhered to.
generation.uncertainty: The precise temperature range and degree of improvement remain uncertain and will require systematic experimental determination. Additionally, the interplay between reduced thermal gradients and possible oxidation or phase instability introduces further uncertainty.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of high-entropy alloy components using LPBF from the same powder batch under identical standard processing conditions aside from the intervention. One set will be fabricated using the standard LPBF process with no preheating (baseline), and the other with in-situ powder bed preheating at 500 °C. Post-fabrication, samples will be examined for dimensional accuracy, defect density (via SEM and CT scans), residual stress (using X-ray or neutron diffraction), and mechanical properties (via compression and hardness tests).
measurements: Dimensional accuracy (quantified by measuring warpage and deviation from CAD specifications)
Defect density and porosity (assessed through scanning electron microscopy and computed tomography)
Residual stress levels (determined using diffraction methods)
Mechanical properties such as yield strength, compressive strength, and hardness
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the preheated samples do not show statistically significant improvements in dimensional precision, reduced defect density, lower residual stress, and enhanced mechanical properties compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: Can refractory high-entropy alloy WTaMoNbV be adequately synthesized via a laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) process using mixed elemental alloying powder as the raw material, and how do its properties compare to a counterpart produced by arc melting furnace (AMF)?. System: Refractory High-Entropy Alloy WTaMoNbV (20 at.% W, 20 at.% Ta, 20 at.% Mo, 20 at.% Nb, 20 at.% V). Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) using EOSINT M290 system (400 W Nd-YAG laser, pure argon atmosphere); mixed elemental powders (20–70 µm) stirred for 6 h at 23 rpm; advanced trials parameters: 244 W laser power, 300 mm/s scanning speed, 0.10 mm hatch spacing, 0.03 mm layer thickness, 162.7 J/mm³ energy density, 67° layer rotation.. Test conditions: Density and Vickers hardness (HV10) measured; compression strength tested at 0.5 mm/min crosshead speed; electrochemical behavior assessed via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5% NaCl solution at ambient temperature (scanning rate 0.5 mV/s)..
